result:
On the last Thursday of every month, Mara repaired umbrellas.

She did it at a little table outside the train station, where commuters hurried past with coffee in their hands and weather on their minds. Most umbrellas needed a new spoke or a few stitches. One had a handle worn smooth by three generations of palms.

A man once asked why she bothered. New umbrellas were cheap.

Mara held up the one she was fixing. Its blue fabric had faded almost gray, except for a bright circle where a sticker had recently been peeled away.

“The owner told me her daughter put that sticker on when she was six,” Mara said. “She’s twenty now.”

The man looked at the umbrella. Then he looked at the dark clouds gathering beyond the station roof. He set his broken one on the table.

Mara opened it carefully. One rib hung loose, but the fabric was sound.

“Come back in ten minutes,” she said.
